17948021463300196.caption:
How my schedule changed as my agency grew:

0-20 clients:

I was doing everything. Fulfillment, strategy, sales calls, content, audits for every brand in the pipeline. All of it ran through me.

This is the phase where you learn the business inside and out because you literally have no choice. You are the business.

20-50 clients:

This is where everything almost broke.

I was still doing fulfillment and managing all the client strategy myself and it wasn't sustainable. So I made the hardest shift: I gave up fulfillment.

Brought on a Director of Ops to take the lead on client work execution.

A big shift was starting hiring people who actually had experience instead of just whoever I could afford. 

Then you get people to oversee them. You build a layer between you and the day-to-day work.

I was able to double down on content, marketing, and sales. Still had my hands in fulfillment a little bit. But the shift was happening.

50-100 clients:

Now I was still working 12-14 hours a day still.

I had to ask myself a real question: what do I keep doing myself?

The answer was marketing. That was the thing that I’m best at and viewed as highest leverage.

My hardest decision was dropping sales… but it was necessary as I was spending 4-5 hours a day on it.

I brought on a closer and spent a stupid amount of time training him up and managing him. Over time though, this become a huge time unlock.

And still, a ton of my time went into hiring and escalations, all while keeping up with all the marketing I was doing. 

100+ clients:

Now it's about building the machine that runs without me in it.

Training up senior team members on email strategy so the quality stays high without me reviewing every account. 

My time goes into content, overall company development, and building new things. 

My next phase is getting sales management off my plate, sales audits off my plate, service development off my plate, and working closely on developing AI systems.

The work never gets less… (I’ve worked 10-12 hours a day every day since I started)…

It just changes.

At every stage you have to be willing to let go of the thing you were good at so you can focus on what you need to grow.

17978876262141245.caption:
Comment “SUBSCRIPTION” for the full 30+ page subscription document! 

1. Get first orders on subscription. First order subscribers are worth 2-3x more than one-time buyers at the 12 month mark. 

2. Front load your subscription offer. Instead of 20% every order, do 30% off first order and 10% recurring. We incentivize first order subscription and save margin on back end. 

3. Auto select subscription on your PDP page. This automatically increases your subscription take rate. Very little effort with high impact. 

4. Align pop-up offer with subscription offer. No need to give an extra discount. Just have your pop-up offer be your best subscription offer. Save margin. 

5. Have a strong email onboarding. Have multiple emails educating on long term usage of product. Get them to use the product every day. And get them to buy in to 6 month+ of usage. 

6. Customize billing reminders emails. Change the framing from “you’re about to be charged” to “get excited, here’s what’s coming”.

7. Customize order confirmation emails. Instead of framing being “you were just charged” make it “congrats, here are the benefits you have”

18113358068324038.caption:
The thing holding your business back is probably you thinking nobody is as good as you.

There was a time I was managing like 20 accounts at one point…

And I kept telling myself that if I handed anything off it would be worse, the client would get a worse experience, and the work would suffer.

So I just held onto everything.

Then one day I literally did not have the time to do it anymore. So I told my account manager to just present their strategy and emails to the client.

I was bracing for the client to be disappointed…

Turns out they loved it. They even told my AM they liked it better than what I had been doing.

That messed with me for a while because in my head their work was WORSE than mine.

But the client didn’t see it that way at all.

It was different for sure.

But different doesn’t always mean worse.

”80% done by someone else is 100% awesome” - Dan Martell

If someone can get something to 80% of how you would do it that’s 100% awesome. Because the time it takes to go from 80 to 100 is not worth it. And most of the time nobody notices the difference except you.

The moment I actually bought into this was when the business started growing.

Because I stopped holding onto everything and started letting people own their work while I could focus on getting clients.

You can’t scale if every piece of output has to go through your brain first.

18039986558839048.caption:
A one-star review feels personal, so the first reply most owners write is a defense. Three paragraphs on why the customer is wrong.

The person who left it is already gone. The people reading your reply are deciding whether to buy from you next week, and they’re reading it to find out what kind of company they’d be dealing with. A long argument tells them more about you than the review did.

So I’d fix the thing first, if it’s real, then write two lines:

You were right. It’s been fixed.

If it isn’t real, the reply is still two lines: stay polite and say what you’d do for them next time.

A quick check: read the last three replies you wrote and ask whether you’d buy from the place that wrote them.

after building email for brands across every niche, these are the principles i keep coming back to every single month:

→ attributed revenue is a skewed metric: your email platform can take credit for sales it didn’t actually drive.

→ plain text beats designed emails: designed emails look beautiful, but plain text cuts through the noise because it reads like a real person wrote it.

→ spend 80% of your time on the hero section: most people never scroll past the first screen, so the top of your email decides whether the rest even gets seen.

→ send more emails: good content doesn’t annoy people, and just like on social media, nobody unfollows a creator for posting great stuff every day.

→ unsubscribes are a good thing: the people leaving were never going to buy, and every unsubscribe helps you land in the inbox for the ones who will.

→ copy paste your winning angles every month: most of your list never saw your best email the first time, so if it worked once it will work again.

→ good popups never hurt conversion rates: bad popups do, but a good one captures visitors who were going to leave anyway.

→ you own your list, not your followers: algorithms change overnight, but your list lets you reach every customer whenever you want.

the point isn’t to follow every email “best practice” you see online, it’s to understand what actually moves revenue and ignore what only looks good in a report.

Sometimes it’s the smallest details that make an email feel more personal.

Retention is what builds a brand… If your customers only buy once, you’re not building a brand. You’re renting them.

→ Your profitability improves

→ You become less dependent on paid advertising to survive.

The brands that win long term aren’t necessarily the ones acquiring the most customers.

That’s how you build a brand, not just a store.

👉 Lessons after generating over $100m+ in email revenue

Lesson 1 — The offer beats the email

You can write the best email in the world, but it won’t work if the deal isn’t exciting.

Example:

A skincare brand sends a beautifully designed email offering 10% off one product. It barely makes any sales.

They change the offer to:

“Buy the full routine and get the cleanser free.”

The copy and design stay almost the same but sales jump because the offer is stronger.

Takeaway: Before rewriting the email, improve what you’re asking people to buy or how you position it.

Lesson 2 — Timing beats frequency

Sending more emails to everyone isn’t as powerful as sending the right email at the right moment.

Example:

A customer views the same protein powder three times but doesn’t buy.

Instead of waiting for the next general campaign, the brand automatically sends:

“Still deciding? Here’s what makes this formula different.”

It answers their questions while the product is still on their mind.

Takeaway: Customer behaviour tells you when and what to send.

Lesson 3 — Your best customers shouldn’t receive the same emails as everyone else

Different customers need different reasons to buy.

Example:

A first-time visitor might need:

“Get 15% off your first order.”

But a loyal customer who has purchased six times doesn’t need another discount. They might respond better to:

“You’ve got early access to our new product.”

One customer needs a reason to try the brand. The other wants recognition and exclusivity.

Takeaway: Change the message based on the customer’s relationship with the brand.

Lesson 4 — Attributed revenue isn’t the same as generated revenue

Email platforms can take credit for orders that the email didn’t actually cause.

Example:

An abandoned-cart flow says it generated $100,000.

The brand excludes a small test group from receiving those emails. That group still spends $70,000 because many customers return and buy anyway.

The email’s true extra impact was closer to $30,000, not the full $100,000 shown in the dashboard.

Takeaway: Measure the extra sales caused by email—not just the sales it received credit for.

Follow these tips to become an email marketing powerhouse 👇

1) Define the customer pain point
If you don’t know what your customer is struggling with, your email is guessing.

2) Make emails that are aesthetic
Good design signals a serious brand. Bad design gets deleted.

3) CTA above the fold
If they have to scroll to find the button, most of them won’t.

4) Create segments for every customer
Talking to everyone means connecting with no one.

5) Send at least 12 emails per month
The brands doing real numbers are sending way more than you think.

6) Check flow performance every week
Your flows print money in the background. Ignoring them is leaving cash on the floor.

7) Turn off smart sending
Klaviyo’s default settings are throttling your reach. Take back control.

8) Implement pattern interrupts
The email that looks different in the inbox is the one that gets opened.

9) Use infographics
Your customers scan. They don’t read. Design accordingly.

10) Reuse your winners
If an email worked once, it’ll work again. Stop reinventing every send.
